//: PLANE 4 — client template (sing-box). Automatic tier failover, zero user decisions.
THE MOST COMMON CAUSE OF TOTAL SYSTEM FAILURE IS NOT BLOCKING.
It is that people did not install the tool, could not configure it, or gave
up when it broke. Every design choice here serves one goal: the user opens
the app, it connects, and it keeps working without them ever learning the
word 'REALITY'.
The 'auto' selector races all tiers and picks whatever currently works.
When Tier D is blocklisted, Tier A takes over silently. When a whitelist
comes down and only CDN traffic survives, Tier A is already the winner.
When everything the operator owns is gone, Tor/Snowflake carries the floor.
Endpoints below are PLACEHOLDERS. In production the client fetches them from
the distributor subscription URL and rewrites this file on every poll.

dns.//: DoH over the tunnel only. A plaintext :53 lookup leaks every destination to the ISP and is trivially hijacked to a block page.

outbounds.//: USER-FACING SELECTOR. The only thing a person would ever touch, and they should not have to.

//: AUTOMATIC FAILOVER. Races every tier and uses the fastest that responds.
interrupt_exist_connections=false so a switch does not drop a live call.
This is what makes burns invisible to the user.
TIER A — CDN-fronted. THE WHITELIST-PROOF PATH.
Terminates at Cloudflare IPs. Blocking it means blocking a large slice
of the working web, including whitelisted sites. Slower than Tier D but
structurally far harder to kill. Listed FIRST on purpose: under
default-deny it is the only thing that survives.
TIER D — direct REALITY. Throughput.
REALITY borrows a real third-party certificate chain, so an active probe
gets a genuine response from the genuine site. This does not make the node
unblockable — it forces the censor from cheap protocol-matching up to
expensive IP enumeration. utls fingerprint is MANDATORY: without it the
ClientHello identifies this as a Go program no matter how good the rest is.
TIER B — the floor. Requires nothing from the operator and cannot be
burned by operator mistakes. Slow, but it is what remains when every
server we run is blocklisted. Point at a local Tor client running
Snowflake or WebTunnel.

route.//: Domestic and private traffic goes direct. Routing local banking through a foreign tunnel is slow, breaks sites, and makes the tunnel conspicuous in traffic analysis.
